11: ---
12: 
13: # mcp-aside-devtools
14: 
15: > Turn browser work into agent work with the Aside AI browser: natural-language tasks that finish goals and a deterministic JavaScript REPL for evidence, with an MCP path for Code Mode composition.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
20: 
21: | Aspect | What you get |
22: |---|---|
23: | **Use it for** | Goal-driven browser-agent tasks and deterministic browser steps (tabs, snapshots, screenshots and PDFs), plus MCP-composed browser work from an agent |
24: | **Invoke with** | "aside", "aside browser", "AI browser automation", "aside cli", "aside mcp" or auto-routing on browser-agent keywords |
25: | **Works on** | macOS (Darwin) arm64/x64 only. The official installer rejects Linux and Windows |
26: | **Produces** | Agent-task outcomes, REPL evaluation results, screenshots, PDFs and snapshots, plus discovered MCP tool fixtures |
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## 2. OVERVIEW
31: 
32: ### Why This Skill Exists
33: 
34: Browser work from an agent splits into two shapes. One is outcome-oriented: multi-step goals like `"sign in, compare, download"`. The other is deterministic evidence: `"open this tab, snapshot it, screenshot it"`. Aside serves both from one binary, a natural-language browser agent and a Playwright-compatible JavaScript REPL, plus a local MCP server for composition with other tools. Picking the wrong lane wastes tokens. Worse, it hands a deterministic proof job to a nondeterministic agent. This skill routes between the lanes and holds the safety lines Aside's identity and permission model requires.
35: 
36: ### What It Does
37: 
38: The `aside` CLI is the primary surface. `aside "<prompt>"` and `aside exec` run agent tasks under a signed-in account with pause and resume approval gates. `aside repl "<JavaScript>"` runs deterministic Playwright-style steps in a persistent context. The Aside MCP server (`aside mcp`, local stdio) is the Code Mode fallback for chaining browser work with other MCP tools. Its live-probed inventory is exactly one `repl` tool on the pinned version, so the skill mandates runtime rediscovery instead of hardcoded tool names.
39: 
40: The MCP transport belongs to `mcp-code-mode`. This skill consumes Code Mode as a provider. Chrome and Chromium CDP debugging stay with `mcp-chrome-devtools`. Aside has no CDP-domain parity. No dedicated console or network capture contract has been verified.
41: 
42: ### The Lane Capability Layer
43: 
44: | Capability | What the skill knows how to operate |
45: |---|---|
46: | **Agent task lane** | multi-step browser goals under a signed-in account, with approval gates and human-only identity boundaries |
47: | **Deterministic REPL lane** | Playwright-compatible JavaScript steps in a persistent context, with `openTab`, `snapshot` and `page.screenshot` helpers |
48: | **MCP composition path** | one `repl` tool over local stdio for chaining browser work with other Code Mode tools |
49: | **DevTools parity** | console and network events through the `page` API, with no native HAR export and no dedicated capture tools |
50: 
51: ### Safety Lines
52: 
53: - One UTCP manual per account and profile, single writer. The parallel-manual strategy is an unresolved research question.
54: - No implicit installs or updates.
55: - Untrusted-content discipline on every page and tool result.
56: - Artifacts verified independently. A screenshot is a non-empty PNG-magic file, not a successful tool response.
57: 
58: ---
59: 
60: ## 3. QUICK START
61: 
62: **Step 1: Install the CLI (macOS only, operator-invoked).**
63: 
64: ```bash
65: curl -fsSL https://releases.aside.com/install.sh | bash
66: ```
67: 
68: **Step 2: Verify the binary and sign-in state.**
69: 
70: ```bash
71: command -v aside
72: # Expected: ~/.local/bin/aside (default shim location)
73: 
74: aside --version 2>&1
75: # Expected: a version string (e.g. 1.26.626.1517)
76: 
77: aside account list 2>&1
78: aside account status 2>&1
79: # Expected: at least one account. Built-in models require active sign-in
80: ```
81: 
82: **Step 3: Run each lane.**
83: 
84: ```bash
85: # Agent task (outcome-oriented)
86: aside "Open https://example.com and summarize the page"
87: 
88: # Deterministic REPL (evidence-oriented)
89: aside repl "openTab('https://example.com')"
90: ```
91: 
92: **Step 4: Use the MCP path with Code Mode.**
93: 
94: The `aside` manual is registered in `.utcp_config.json` (dated 2026-07-16, snapshot in [`assets/utcp-aside-manual.md`](./assets/utcp-aside-manual.md)). Live discovery confirmed the callable the same day (fixture: [`references/discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json`](./references/discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json)). Discovery lists the registry name `aside.aside.repl` with dots. The TypeScript call inside `call_tool_chain` is `aside.aside_repl(args)`. Re-verify per session because `tools.listChanged` is true:
95: 
96: ```typescript
97: call_tool_chain(`
98:   const result = await aside.aside_repl({
99:     title: "Open example.com",
100:     code: "await openTab('https://example.com'); console.log(await snapshot(page));"
101:   });
102:   return result;
103: `)
104: ```
105: 
106: ---
107: 
108: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
109: 
110: ### The Routing Rule
111: 
112: The skill prefers the CLI. Outcome-oriented requests route to the agent-task lane. Deterministic proof requests route to the REPL lane. Composition with other Code Mode tools routes to the MCP path. A weighted intent scorer reads the request text and loads only the reference files relevant to the chosen lane.
113: 
114: ### The CLI Paths
115: 
116: The agent-task lane (`aside "<task>"`, `aside exec`, `--session <id>` continuation, `--account <id>` selection) covers navigation, DOM inspection, screenshots, downloads, file use, approval requests and password-manager sign-in. MFA/CAPTCHA/vault boundaries stay human-only. The REPL lane (`aside repl`) keeps a persistent JavaScript context with Playwright APIs and helpers such as `openTab(url)`, `snapshot(page)`, `page.screenshot(options)` and `annotatedScreenshot`.
117: 
118: ### The MCP Path
119: 
120: `aside mcp` is a client-spawned local stdio process with no credential field. It inherits the logged-in CLI context. On the live-probed version (`1.26.626.1517`, protocol `2024-11-05`) the inventory is exactly one `repl` tool with `title` and `code` inputs and a 120-second timeout. `tools.listChanged: true` makes that inventory version-pinned evidence: rediscover at runtime, always. A fresh MCP process is browser-unbound until a task or profile binding exists. That error is a binding state, not an auth failure.
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
125: 
126: ### When To Use This Skill
127: 
128: Reach for this skill when browser work should run through the Aside AI browser: agent-delegated multi-step goals, deterministic REPL evidence, MCP-composed browser work and Aside-account-backed sessions. Reach for `mcp-chrome-devtools` when the job is imperative CDP debugging or HAR export. Reach for Playwright/Puppeteer/Selenium for cross-browser test frameworks.
129: 
130: ### Related Skills
131: 
132: | Skill | Relationship |
133: |---|---|
134: | `mcp-code-mode` | Owns the MCP transport. Aside is registered as a Code Mode provider (the `aside` manual) and is called through `call_tool_chain()` after discovery confirmation. |
135: | `mcp-chrome-devtools` | Sibling packet for Chrome CDP debugging (`bdg`). Routing discipline is shared. Command surfaces are not. |
136: | `sk-code` | Owns application-code standards and tests for the code being verified in the browser. |
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
141: 
142: | What you see | Why | Fix |
143: |---|---|---|

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES
235: 
236: ### Create Reference File When
237: 
238: **Workflow Complexity**:
239: - Multi-phase workflows with validation checkpoints
240: - Decision trees with multiple branches
241: - Pattern libraries with 5+ variations
242: - Systematic debugging procedures
243: 
244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes
249: 
250: **Size Threshold**:
251: - Content exceeds 200 lines
252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed
254: 
255: ### Keep in SKILL.md When
256: 
257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
261:   > **Note**: RULES sections in SKILL.md use ALL-CAPS H3 headers: `### ALWAYS`, `### NEVER`, `### ESCALATE IF` (or `####` at phase depth). See [skill-md-template.md](./skill-md-template.md) for the complete pattern.
262: - Quick reference
263: 
264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines
265: 
266: ### Reference File Types for AI Agent Skills
267: 
268: | Type                | Purpose                                | Example (kebab-case)          | Size           |
269: | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- |
270: | **Workflow**        | Multi-phase processes with checkpoints | `implementation-workflows.md` | 500-1500 lines |
271: | **Pattern Library** | Code patterns with before/after        | `shared-patterns.md`          | 300-800 lines  |
272: | **Standards**       | Rules and conventions                  | `code-quality-standards.md`   | 400-1000 lines |
273: | **Debugging**       | Systematic troubleshooting             | `debugging-workflows.md`      | 600-1200 lines |
274: | **Tool Guide**      | MCP/external tool integration          | `devtools-guide.md`           | 200-600 lines  |
275: | **Quick Reference** | Commands, shortcuts, checklists        | `quick-reference.md`          | 200-400 lines  |
276: 
277: **Note:** All authored reference file names use kebab-case (hyphens, lowercase).
278: 
279: ---
280: 
281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
300: 
301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```
305: 
306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"
309: - "Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history"
310: 
311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312: 
313: **Purpose**: Structured processes with mandatory checkpoints
314: 
315: **Format**:
316: ```markdown
317: ### The [Number] Phases
318: 
319: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
320: 
321: #### Phase 1: [Phase Name]
322: 
323: **Purpose**: [What this phase accomplishes]
324: 
325: **Actions**:
326: 1. [Action 1]
327: 2. [Action 2]
328: 
329: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
330: 
331: #### Phase 2: [Phase Name]
332: 
333: [Similar structure]
334: ```
335: 
336: **Key Elements**:
337: - **"You MUST complete"** - Mandatory language
338: - **Named checkpoints** - `checkpoint_name` for validation
339: - **Sequential phases** - Cannot skip ahead
340: 
341: ### Before/After Code Examples
342: 
343: **Purpose**: Show transformation from wrong to right
344: 
345: **Format**:
346: ```markdown
347: ### [Pattern Name]
348: 
349: **BEFORE**: [Problem description]
350: \```[language]
351: // Bad code with issues
352: // Showing what NOT to do
353: \```
354: 
355: **AFTER**: [Solution description]
356: \```[language]
357: // Good code with fixes
358: // Showing correct approach
359: \```
360: 
361: **Why better**: [Explanation of improvement]
362: ```
363: 
364: **Key Elements**:
365: - `BEFORE:` marker for the wrong-way code
366: - `AFTER:` marker for the right-way code
367: - Inline comments explaining issues
368: - "Why better" rationale
369: 
370: ### Pattern Comparison Tables
371: 
372: **Purpose**: Compare approaches across scenarios
373: 
374: **Format**:
375: ```markdown
376: ### Common Patterns
377: 
378: | Scenario     | Approach A (Wrong) | Approach B (Right) | Why Better  |
379: | ------------ | ------------------ | ------------------ | ----------- |
380: | [Scenario 1] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
381: | [Scenario 2] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
382: ```
383: 
384: **Use when**: Multiple scenarios need comparison
385: 
386: ### Decision Logic in Markdown
387: 
388: **Purpose**: Explicit if/then logic for workflow decisions
389: 
390: **Format**:
391: \```markdown
392: ### Decision Logic
393: 
394: \```markdown
395: IF [condition A]:
396:   → [Action/Path A]
397:   → [Expected outcome A]
398: 
399: IF [condition B]:
400:   → [Action/Path B]
401:   → [Expected outcome B]
402: 
403: IF [condition C]:
404:   → [Action/Path C]
405:   → [Expected outcome C]

407: \```

409: **Alternative format** (decision tree):
410: \```markdown
411: \```
412: Analyze situation
413: ├─ Condition A met
414: │  └─ Execute Workflow A
415: │     └─ Expected outcome A
416: ├─ Condition B met
417: │  └─ Execute Workflow B
418: │     └─ Expected outcome B

423: \```
424: 
425: ### Validation Checkpoints
426: 
427: **Purpose**: Named checkpoints throughout workflows
428: 
429: **Format**:
430: ```markdown
431: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
432: ```
433:

435: - `files_analyzed`

437: - `strategy_determined`
438: - `root_cause_identified`
439: 
440: **Usage**: Reference in quality checklists and debugging

445:

451: 
452: [1-2 sentence summary only - no prerequisites here]
453: 
454: ---
455: 
456: \## 1. OVERVIEW
457:

477:

479:

491: - [Expected output 1]
492: - [Expected output 2]
493:

501: \```
502: 
503: **Format for Scripts**:
504: ```markdown

506: ```
507: 
508: **Format for Assets**:

513: ### Common Error Patterns
514: 
515: **Purpose**: Document actual errors with explanations
516: 
517: **Format**:
518: \```markdown
519: **Common [System/Browser] Errors:**
520: 
521: \```javascript
522: // [Actual error message]
523: // → [What it means]
524: // → [How to fix]
525: 
526: // [Another error message]
527: // → [What it means]
528: // → [How to fix]
529: \```
530: \```
531: 
532: **Example**:

535: 
536: \```javascript
537: // Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read property 'X' of undefined
538: // → Variable is undefined, check initialization
539: // → Verify element exists before accessing properties

541: // Failed to load resource: net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT

545: \```

549: **Purpose**: Explicitly state what's in/out of scope

551: **Format**:

554: 
555: **Out of scope:** [What is NOT supported]
556: ```

567: **Purpose**: Specific viewport tests with checkboxes

584: ### Phased Workflow with Checkpoints Example

621:       - "Add necessary tests"
622:       - "Update documentation"

624:     validation_questions:
625:       - "Do all tests pass?"
626:       - "Is code documented?"
627:       - "Are standards followed?"
628: 
629:   phase_4_validation:
630:     purpose: "Verify correctness and quality"
631:     depends_on: "phase_3_implementation"
632:     actions:
633:       - "Run full test suite"
634:       - "Check code quality metrics"
635:       - "Review against requirements"
636:     checkpoint: "quality_verified"
637:     validation_questions:
638:       - "Do all tests pass?"
639:       - "Are quality metrics met?"
640:       - "Does this satisfy the original request?"
641: ```
642: 
643: **Example in Markdown Reference**:
644: ```markdown
645: ### Implementation Workflow
646: 
647: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
648: 
649: #### Phase 1: Preparation
650: 
651: **Purpose**: Gather context and analyze requirements
652: 
653: **Actions**:
654: 1. Read user request carefully
655: 2. Identify affected files and systems
656: 3. Review relevant documentation
657: 
658: **Validation**: `requirements_understood`

661: - Are there any unclear requirements?

670: 3. Plan validation strategy

672: **Validation**: `design_approved`
673: - Is this the simplest approach?
674: - Have I considered edge cases?
675: - Can I test this effectively?
676: 
677: [Continue with remaining phases...]
678: ```
679: 
680: ---
681: 
682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882: 
883: ---
884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---

1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.

77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79:

81:

83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages

193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882:

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986:

15: # Aside CLI Reference
16: 
17: Operational reference for the `aside` binary: the natural-language agent-task lane, the deterministic REPL lane, account management, and the option surface — with every claim traced to published docs or a live help fixture, and every unresolved point marked UNKNOWN.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: Aside is an AI browser with a real standalone macOS CLI, not merely an MCP server. The installed binary exposes agent tasks (`aside "<task>"`, `aside exec`), a deterministic Playwright-compatible browser JavaScript REPL (`aside repl`), account management (`aside account ...`), and a local MCP server launcher (`aside mcp`). Subcommands observed on version `1.26.626.1517` are exactly `account`, `exec`, `repl`, and `mcp`.
24: 
25: The command surface is **version-pinned evidence**. Re-capture `aside --version` and `aside --help` (plus per-subcommand `--help`) as fixtures before relying on any flag, and prefer the installed help over documentation examples when they disagree.
26: 
27: ---
28: 
29: ## 2. COMMAND SURFACE
30: 
31: ### Verified Commands
32: 
33: | Command | Purpose |
34: |---|---|
35: | `aside "<task>"` | Start a natural-language browser-agent task (primary surface) |
36: | `aside --session <id> "<task>"` | Continue a prior task/session |
37: | `aside --account <id> "<task>"` | Run a direct task under a selected account |
38: | `aside exec ...` | Explicit task execution with provider/model controls |
39: | `aside account list` | Enumerate accounts |
40: | `aside account status [id]` | Inspect an account |
41: | `aside account use <id>` | Select the account |
42: | `aside repl "<JavaScript>"` | Deterministic browser automation (e.g. `openTab(...)`) |
43: | `aside mcp` | Start the local MCP server over stdio |
44: 
45: If no command is given, Aside starts a browser-agent session; passing a URL opens that page in Aside (observed on the installed help fixture).
46: 
47: ### Top-Level Options (observed on 1.26.626.1517)
48: 
49: ```text
50: --version | --session <id> | --account <id> | --model <model> | --provider <provider>
51: --speed <default|fast> | --effort <off|minimal|low|medium|high|xhigh|ultrabrowse> | --update
52: ```
53: 
54: `--update` exists but must stay operator-invoked; never run updates or the installer implicitly.
55: 
56: ### UNKNOWN: Model-Flag Spelling
57: 
58: Documentation examples show `aside exec --account u1 -m openai-codex/gpt-5.5` (a combined `-m provider/model` convention), while the installed `--help` shows separate `--model <model>` and `--provider <provider>` options with no `-m` recorded. This is unresolved — likely a docs-example alias versus installed-help difference. Capture the installed version's help before freezing either spelling in a script.
59: 
60: ---
61: 
62: ## 3. LANE SELECTION
63: 
64: ### Agent-Task Lane
65: 
66: Use `aside "<prompt>"` or `aside exec` for goal-driven, multi-step, approval-gated, credential-autofill, or multi-site work. Documented agent capabilities: navigate, page/DOM inspection, screenshots, downloads, browse/search, use files, search history, request approvals, sign in via password-manager autofill, wait for notifications, and create/preview files (images/PDFs/HTML/text).
67: 
68: ### Deterministic REPL Lane
69: 
70: Use `aside repl "<JavaScript>"` for direct inspection, screenshots, downloads, and repeatable evidence-producing steps. The documented example pattern is `openTab(...)`. The REPL keeps a persistent JavaScript context while its process is alive.
71: 
72: Helper surface of the MCP `repl` tool, confirmed by live Code Mode discovery 2026-07-16 ([`discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json`](./discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json); supersedes the earlier version-pinned advertised list; the CLI REPL is documented as the same deterministic lane):
73: - Console and display: `console.log`, `display(input)`
74: - Browser state: `page`, `tabs`
75: - Tab helpers: `listBrowserTabs()`, `attachBrowserTab(targetId)`, `attachActiveBrowserTab()`, `getTabByTargetId(targetId)`, `openTab(url)`, `closeTab(tab)`
76: - Evidence: `snapshot(page, options?)`, `page.screenshot(options?)`, `locator.screenshot(options?)`, `page.pdf(options?)`, `annotatedScreenshot(page)`
77: - Node and utilities: `fs` (`node:fs/promises`), `pwd`, `path`, `Buffer`, `sleep(ms)`, `fetch(url)`
78: 
79: A non-mutating probe had earlier confirmed `page`, `tabs`, `fs`, `pwd` as values and `openTab`, `snapshot`, `annotatedScreenshot`, `fetch` as functions.
80: 
81: **UNKNOWN**: the exact output shapes of `snapshot` and screenshots on a *bound* page are untested (discovery lists the surface; it does not exercise calls). Treat every helper call's result shape as probe-required until exercised.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## 4. BOUNDARY RULES
86: 
87: 1. `--account` is documented for direct tasks and `exec` only — do not invent `aside mcp --account` or `aside repl --account`; `aside mcp --help` exposes no account/session option.
88: 2. `--session` belongs to agent-task continuation; it is not an MCP browser-target selector.
89: 3. There are no typed `aside navigate`, `aside dom`, `aside screenshot`, `aside console`, or `aside network` subcommands — deterministic work goes through the REPL.
90: 4. Whether `repl` or `mcp` can select an account without changing the global default is UNKNOWN.
91: 5. Quote the entire task prompt or REPL JavaScript as a single shell argument; capture stderr with `2>&1`.
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 5. ACCOUNTS AND PROVIDERS
96: 
97: Provider tiers (Settings > AI > Providers): **Aside built-in** (plan-included models, requires active cloud sign-in), **Subscription** (OAuth reuse of ChatGPT Plus/Pro, Claude Pro/Max, GitHub Copilot), and **API** (BYO keys: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, xAI, Vercel AI Gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway).
98: 
99: Sign-out behavior: a warning is printed; BYO provider keys keep working, built-in models fail closed until re-sign-in. Recover with `aside account use <id>` or per-run `--account`. Model-provider credentials are not MCP transport credentials — the MCP surface has no published credential field.
100: 
101: ---
102: 
103: ## 6. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
104: 
105: - [session-management.md](./session-management.md) — three-layer session model, daemon, concurrency, permission modes.
106: - [mcp-wiring.md](./mcp-wiring.md) — MCP transport, discovery, and Code Mode registration posture.
107: - [troubleshooting.md](./troubleshooting.md) — error taxonomy and recovery flows.
108: - Primary sources: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers>, <https://docs.aside.com/help/ai>, <https://docs.aside.com/help/tasks>.

46: ## 3. CLI COMMAND SURFACE
47: 
48: **CONFIRMED (S1, S2, S4)** — the online docs corroborate the version-pinned surface already captured in [`aside-cli-reference.md`](aside-cli-reference.md); nothing new was added or removed:
49: 
50: - `aside "<task>"` — start a natural-language browser-agent session. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
51: - `aside --session <session-id> "<task>"` — continue an existing session. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
52: - `aside --account <id> "<task>"` — target a specific account for a single run (documented for `aside` and `aside exec`). [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
53: - `aside account list` — list accounts (current marked with `*`). [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
54: - `aside account status [id]` — show current or specific account status. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
55: - `aside account use <id>` — set the default account for future commands. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
56: - `aside mcp` — launch MCP server mode. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
57: - `aside repl "<code>"` — execute deterministic browser-automation REPL code. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
58: 
59: **UNKNOWN — model-flag spelling.** The public docs do not resolve the `-m provider/model` vs separate `--model` / `--provider` conflict noted in SKILL.md. Still capture the installed `aside --help` before relying on either. [SOURCE: not present in S1–S5]
60: 
61: **CONFIRMED — example agent tasks (S4)**, useful as realistic task-lane prompts:
62: 
63: - `aside "Open the failed GitHub Actions run for this PR, find the first failing step, compare it with the last passing run, and draft a PR comment with log links. Do not post it."`
64: - `aside "Open localhost:3000, run through signup, capture desktop and mobile screenshots, and write a short QA note."`
65: 
66: Both examples end with an explicit "do not post / do not change settings" boundary — the docs repeatedly steer developers to keep Aside read-oriented and leave code changes in the coding agent. [SOURCE: <https://aside.com/blog/developers>]

70: ## 4. MCP SERVER (`aside mcp`)
71: 
72: **CONFIRMED (S2)** — the docs give an explicit `mcp.json` wiring block, verbatim:
73: 
74: ```json
75: {
76:   "mcpServers": {
77:     "aside": {
78:       "command": "aside",
79:       "args": ["mcp"]
80:     }
81:   }
82: }
83: ```
84: 
85: [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
86: 
87: - **CONFIRMED** — purpose framing: `"Use aside mcp to connect Aside to another agent or coding tool as a Model Context Protocol server."` [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers.md>]
88: - **CONFIRMED** — MCP use case (S4): reach for MCP "when your coding agent needs evidence from private browser pages, such as a CI log, feature-flag dashboard, Datadog trace, internal admin page, or staging screenshot." [SOURCE: <https://aside.com/blog/developers>]
89: - **INFERRED** — transport is local stdio launched by the client as `command: aside, args: ["mcp"]` (no URL/port/token field in the config), matching the direct-stdio probe already recorded in [`mcp-wiring.md`](mcp-wiring.md) and the fixture. [SOURCE: S2 config shape + `discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json`]
90: - **CONFIRMED (fixture)** — the exposed tool inventory is exactly one tool, `repl`; Code Mode registry name `aside.aside.repl`, TS callable `aside.aside_repl(args)`. The online docs do not enumerate tools, so the fixture stays the authority. [SOURCE: `discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json`]
91: - **UNKNOWN** — which permission mode the spawned `aside mcp` process inherits. S3 confirms modes exist and that per-session settings layer on agent defaults, but does not state the MCP process's default mode. [SOURCE: partial in S3]

95: ## 5. REPL ENVIRONMENT AND HELPER API
96: 
97: **CONFIRMED (S1, S4)** — the docs describe the REPL as Playwright-shaped: "It feels like Playwright: you get `page`, tabs, locators, screenshots, downloads, and JavaScript," plus "the same page snapshots and stable element refs that the browser agent uses, so a click or assertion lines up with what Aside will actually act on." [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers> ; <https://aside.com/blog/developers>]
98: 
99: **CONFIRMED (fixture)** — the online prose is corroborated and made precise by the live tool schema. The full helper surface (authoritative) is in [`discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json`](discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json) `search_tools[0].description`:
100: 
101: - Environment: ES2023+, `async`/`await`, 120s timeout, **no `import`/`require`**, persistent shared scope across calls (use fresh variable names each call).
102: - Globals: `page` (Playwright Page of the last opened tab), `tabs` (`Page[]`), `console.log(x)` (the ONLY way to return data — `return`/last-expression does NOT work), `display(input)` (render image bytes/base64/data-URL), `fs` (`node:fs/promises`), `path`, `Buffer`, `pwd`, `sleep(ms)`, `fetch(url)` (HTTP with the user's cookies).
103: - Tab helpers: `openTab(url)`, `closeTab(tab)`, `listBrowserTabs()`, `attachBrowserTab(targetId)`, `attachActiveBrowserTab()`, `getTabByTargetId(targetId)`.
104: - Read/evidence helpers: `snapshot(page, options?)` (PRIMARY read method → `{ tree, diff }`), `page.screenshot(options?)`, `locator.screenshot(options?)` (default type `webp`, `margin` default 8), `page.pdf(options?)` (Playwright PDF options; save under `./artifacts/`), `annotatedScreenshot(page)` (PNG with ref-ID labels).
105: 
106: **INFERRED — the capability envelope.** Because `page` is a real Playwright `Page`, the standard Playwright `page`/`context`/`browser` API is reachable inside the repl even where a helper is not pre-named: `page.$` / `page.$$` / `page.$eval` / `page.evaluate` / `page.content()`, `page.on('console'|'request'|'response'|'requestfinished', …)`, `page.context().cookies()` / `addCookies()`, `page.goto()` / `page.waitForLoadState()`, `page.setViewportSize()`. This is the grounding for the DevTools-parity feature files. It is INFERRED (from the documented "Playwright API available" + real `Page` object), not from a per-method online enumeration; treat each as pattern-documented-but-live-unconfirmed until a bound-session run captures its result shape. [SOURCE: `discovery-fixture-2026-07-16.json` "Playwright API available" + globals list]
107: 
108: ---
109: 
110: ## 6. PERMISSION AND ACCESS MODEL
111: 
112: **CONFIRMED (S3)** — corroborates and sharpens SKILL.md §3:
113: 
114: - Three session permission modes: **Read only** (inspect browser + file context, no file changes), **Guard** (default; work in approved folders, ask before others), **Full access** (read/write anywhere). [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/security.md>]
115: - Three rule values: **Allow** (use without asking), **Ask** (ask first), **Deny** (block; **takes precedence**). [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/security.md>]
116: - **CONFIRMED** — "Saved password values stay hidden from the AI agent"; the system checks password-access policy and target URL before building autofill payloads. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/security.md>]
117: - **CONFIRMED** — layering: "When a task has its own permission settings, Aside applies those task settings on top of the agent defaults." Permission areas span sandbox, readable/writable file roots, and tool/browser/network rules. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/security.md>]
118: - **UNKNOWN** — exact MFA / CAPTCHA / vault-unlock pause semantics are not spelled out in S3; SKILL.md's "human-only boundary" posture stands as the safe default, not a doc-quoted contract. [SOURCE: not detailed in S3]
119: 
120: ---
121: 
122: ## 7. DISTRIBUTION AND VERSIONING
123: 
124: - **CONFIRMED** — install is the operator-invoked curl bootstrap: `curl -fsSL https://releases.aside.com/install.sh | bash`. [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/help/developers>]
125: - **CONFIRMED** — no official public npm or GitHub package for the Aside AI browser's CLI/MCP was found. The two GitHub repos named "aside" (`alxclark/aside` — a browser-extension boilerplate; `google/aside` — an unrelated Google tool) are NOT this product. Distribution is the installer only; there is no `npx`-style MCP launch (contrast `mcp-chrome-devtools`, which launches `chrome-devtools-mcp` via `npx`). [SOURCE: web search 2026-07-17; <https://github.com/alxclark/aside> ; <https://github.com/google/aside>]
126: - **CONFIRMED** — the native browser changelog (S5) latest entry is **v1.0.714.1** (most recent), prior dated entry **v1.0.626.1 (2026-06-26)**; entries are browser-shell/rendering/bookmark fixes. **No CLI, MCP, REPL, permission, or Playwright-surface change is documented since 2026-07-16.** [SOURCE: <https://docs.aside.com/changelog/native>]
127: - **Version-number note.** The native changelog versioning (`v1.0.714.1`) differs from the CLI/MCP build string observed by probe (`1.26.626.1517`). These appear to be separate version lines (browser shell vs CLI/agent build). INFERRED — do not equate them; pin each independently. [SOURCE: S5 vs fixture]
128:

131: ## 8. WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE PRIOR RESEARCH
132: 
133: | Item | Prior packet state | 2026-07-17 finding |
134: |---|---|---|
135: | `mcp.json` wiring | Described as stdio, no verbatim config | **CONFIRMED verbatim** `{"mcpServers":{"aside":{"command":"aside","args":["mcp"]}}}` (S2) |
136: | Permission modes | Stated in SKILL.md, lightly sourced | **CONFIRMED** against `security.md` (S3): Read only / Guard / Full access + Allow / Ask / Deny (Deny wins) |
137: | Console/network capture | Flagged UNKNOWN "no verified contract" | Playwright `page.on(...)` event API is **available** per the fixture — pattern now documentable; live capture still needs a bound session (see DevTools-parity feature files) |
138: | npm/GitHub presence | Not previously checked | **CONFIRMED none** — installer-only distribution |
139: | Dev-surface changelog | — | **No change** since 2026-07-16 (S5) |
140: 
141: ---
142: 
143: ## 9. OPEN UNKNOWNS (UNCHANGED OR NEWLY CONFIRMED-OPEN)
144: 
145: 1. Browser-profile binding procedure for a fresh `aside mcp` process — still undocumented (not in S1–S5).
146: 2. Which permission mode `aside mcp` inherits — S3 confirms the model but not the MCP default.
147: 3. `-m` vs `--model`/`--provider` flag spelling — unresolved online; capture installed `--help`.
148: 4. Live result shapes for the Playwright DevTools-parity patterns (console/network/cookies/performance) — the API is present; no bound-session capture fixture exists yet, so those playbook scenarios stay SKIP-valid until run against an authorized session.

15: # Aside Session Management
16: 
17: State, permissions, lifecycle, and concurrency reference for Aside operations.
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: The state model behind every Aside operation: which layer holds the state, how long it lives, which permissions gate it, and what is safe to run in parallel.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: Use this reference to identify the active state layer, permission boundary, and safe concurrency posture before running an Aside operation.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. THREE-LAYER SESSION MODEL
32: 
33: | Layer | Carrier | Lifetime | Notes |
34: |---|---|---|---|
35: | Agent-task continuation | `--session <id>` on `aside` / `aside exec` | Account-scoped, persists across CLI invocations | Transcripts live in the task folder; generated files persist; tasks can pause for input/approval/notification and resume |
36: | REPL persistence | `aside repl` / the MCP `repl` tool | While the owning process is alive | Persistent JavaScript context (variables survive between evaluations in one process) |
37: | Browser-profile binding | Aside browser task/profile | Bound per task | Browser operations require a binding; a fresh `aside mcp` process is transport-healthy but browser-unbound |
38: 
39: Do not mix the layers: `--session` continues an agent task; it does not select an MCP browser target. The MCP surface exposes no session selector.
40: 
41: **UNKNOWN**: where and how `--session` state is persisted (storage backend) is not publicly documented.
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 3. TASK MODES AND PERMISSIONS
46: 
47: - Task modes: `Default` (normal browser profile) or `Incognito`.
48: - Permission modes: **Read only / Guard (default for new tasks) / Full access**. Full access never exposes saved password values to the agent.
49: - Layered rules: agent-level plus session-level overrides with values `Allow` / `Ask` / `Deny`; Deny takes precedence. Permission areas cover sandbox, readable/writable file roots, reads/writes outside roots, and tool/browser/network rules.
50: - Password boundary: Aside can sign in via password-manager autofill, but saved password values stay hidden from the agent; Aside checks password-access policy and the target URL before building an autofill payload. MFA, passkeys, CAPTCHA, and vault unlock remain human-only boundaries.
51: 
52: **UNKNOWN**: which permission/task mode `aside mcp` inherits, and whether MCP activity is auditable in the Aside UI, is not published. Apply caller-owned read/action/sensitive policy on top.
53: 
54: Data egress: selected prompts, tool results, snapshots, screenshots, and files may reach hosted model providers — "local-first" is not "never leaves device". Redact sensitive material from default logs.
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 4. UNATTENDED USE
59: 
60: "Unattended" is best-effort after a signed-in profile and permission policy are prepared, never a guarantee. MFA, CAPTCHA, identity verification, vault unlock, and approvals can pause a task and require the user to resume. Design workflows for **resumable waiting**, not bypasses: detect the pause, report what the task is waiting on, and hand control to the operator.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ## 5. DAEMON AND PROCESS LIFECYCLE
65: 
66: The MCP child fronts a separate local daemon-backed service (idle-survival and daemon-outage fixes appear in the vendor changelog; connection failures preserve stderr and timeout details). A wrapper must distinguish:
67: - a **dead stdio child** (process exited; respawn is reasonable), from
68: - an **unavailable/incompatible Aside daemon or browser** (respawning the child will not help; escalate).
69: 
70: The public CLI exposes no `daemon`, `status`, or `stop` command and no MCP session-selection command. Rely only on the supported stdio process lifecycle: spawn `aside mcp`, speak JSON-RPC over stdio, and close the process for cleanup.
71: 
72: Observed idle telemetry on `1.26.626.1517`: `discoveryIdleTimeoutMs: 300000` (5 min), `replIdleTimeoutMs: 1800000` (30 min). These are diagnostic observations; their stability across releases is UNKNOWN.
73: 
74: ---

15: # Aside Session Management
16: 
17: State, permissions, lifecycle, and concurrency reference for Aside operations.
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: The state model behind every Aside operation: which layer holds the state, how long it lives, which permissions gate it, and what is safe to run in parallel.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: Use this reference to identify the active state layer, permission boundary, and safe concurrency posture before running an Aside operation.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. THREE-LAYER SESSION MODEL
32: 
33: | Layer | Carrier | Lifetime | Notes |
34: |---|---|---|---|
35: | Agent-task continuation | `--session <id>` on `aside` / `aside exec` | Account-scoped, persists across CLI invocations | Transcripts live in the task folder; generated files persist; tasks can pause for input/approval/notification and resume |
36: | REPL persistence | `aside repl` / the MCP `repl` tool | While the owning process is alive | Persistent JavaScript context (variables survive between evaluations in one process) |
37: | Browser-profile binding | Aside browser task/profile | Bound per task | Browser operations require a binding; a fresh `aside mcp` process is transport-healthy but browser-unbound |
38: 
39: Do not mix the layers: `--session` continues an agent task; it does not select an MCP browser target. The MCP surface exposes no session selector.
40: 
41: **UNKNOWN**: where and how `--session` state is persisted (storage backend) is not publicly documented.
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 3. TASK MODES AND PERMISSIONS
46: 
47: - Task modes: `Default` (normal browser profile) or `Incognito`.
48: - Permission modes: **Read only / Guard (default for new tasks) / Full access**. Full access never exposes saved password values to the agent.
49: - Layered rules: agent-level plus session-level overrides with values `Allow` / `Ask` / `Deny`; Deny takes precedence. Permission areas cover sandbox, readable/writable file roots, reads/writes outside roots, and tool/browser/network rules.
50: - Password boundary: Aside can sign in via password-manager autofill, but saved password values stay hidden from the agent; Aside checks password-access policy and the target URL before building an autofill payload. MFA, passkeys, CAPTCHA, and vault unlock remain human-only boundaries.
51: 
52: **UNKNOWN**: which permission/task mode `aside mcp` inherits, and whether MCP activity is auditable in the Aside UI, is not published. Apply caller-owned read/action/sensitive policy on top.
53: 
54: Data egress: selected prompts, tool results, snapshots, screenshots, and files may reach hosted model providers — "local-first" is not "never leaves device". Redact sensitive material from default logs.
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 4. UNATTENDED USE
59: 
60: "Unattended" is best-effort after a signed-in profile and permission policy are prepared, never a guarantee. MFA, CAPTCHA, identity verification, vault unlock, and approvals can pause a task and require the user to resume. Design workflows for **resumable waiting**, not bypasses: detect the pause, report what the task is waiting on, and hand control to the operator.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ## 5. DAEMON AND PROCESS LIFECYCLE
65: 
66: The MCP child fronts a separate local daemon-backed service (idle-survival and daemon-outage fixes appear in the vendor changelog; connection failures preserve stderr and timeout details). A wrapper must distinguish:
67: - a **dead stdio child** (process exited; respawn is reasonable), from
68: - an **unavailable/incompatible Aside daemon or browser** (respawning the child will not help; escalate).
69: 
70: The public CLI exposes no `daemon`, `status`, or `stop` command and no MCP session-selection command. Rely only on the supported stdio process lifecycle: spawn `aside mcp`, speak JSON-RPC over stdio, and close the process for cleanup.
71: 
72: Observed idle telemetry on `1.26.626.1517`: `discoveryIdleTimeoutMs: 300000` (5 min), `replIdleTimeoutMs: 1800000` (30 min). These are diagnostic observations; their stability across releases is UNKNOWN.
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 6. CONCURRENCY POSTURE
77: 
78: There is no public guarantee for concurrent mutating MCP clients on one profile. Aside routines avoid overlap, and Aside has no documented equivalent of Chrome DevTools' `--isolated=true`.
79: 
80: Default posture:
81: - **Single-writer lock keyed by account/profile.**
82: - Enable read-only concurrency only after a controlled multi-client test proves isolation.
83: - Do not register parallel UTCP manuals (`aside_1`/`aside_2`) — the strategy is an unresolved open question pending that isolation test.
84: 
85: ---
